name: Biogeochemical Cycles – Parts, Types & Carbon Cycle

notes.heading: Overview
points: Biogeochemical cycles describe movement of elements between living organisms and the physical environment
They ensure recycling of essential nutrients in ecosystems
Unlike energy, nutrients are continuously recycled
Major cycles include carbon, nitrogen, water, phosphorus, and sulfur

notes.heading: Biogeochemical Cycle – Meaning
points: Bio = living organisms, Geo = earth, Chemical = elements
Biogeochemical cycles are pathways through which chemical elements circulate
They move between biosphere, lithosphere, atmosphere, and hydrosphere
Maintains balance of nutrients in ecosystems
Essential for sustaining life on Earth

notes.heading: Parts of a Biogeochemical Cycle
points: Reservoir pool – where elements are stored in large amounts (e.g., rocks, atmosphere)
Exchange pool – where elements are actively cycling (plants, animals, soil)
Biotic components – plants, animals, microorganisms
Abiotic components – air, water, soil, rocks
Flux – movement of elements between pools

notes.heading: Reservoir and Exchange Pools
points: Reservoir pool – slow cycling, long-term storage (e.g., carbon in rocks)
Exchange pool – rapid cycling between organisms and environment
Atmosphere is major reservoir for gases like CO₂
Soil acts as both reservoir and exchange medium
Oceans are major carbon and water reservoirs

notes.heading: Types of Biogeochemical Cycles
points: Gaseous cycles – main reservoir is atmosphere (carbon, nitrogen, oxygen cycle)
Sedimentary cycles – main reservoir is earth’s crust (phosphorus, sulfur cycle)
Hydrological cycle – movement of water between land, air, and oceans
Fast cycling – water and carbon (short time scale)
Slow cycling – phosphorus (long geological time scale)

notes.heading: Gaseous Cycles
points: Main reservoir is atmosphere
Elements cycle quickly between living organisms and air
Examples: carbon cycle, nitrogen cycle, oxygen cycle
Highly dynamic and fast-moving cycles
Strongly influenced by human activities

notes.heading: Sedimentary Cycles
points: Main reservoir is earth’s crust (rocks and soil)
Slow cycling process compared to gaseous cycles
Examples: phosphorus cycle, sulfur cycle
Movement occurs through weathering and erosion
Less affected by atmospheric changes

notes.heading: Carbon Cycle – Meaning
points: Carbon cycle describes movement of carbon among atmosphere, biosphere, oceans, and lithosphere
Carbon is fundamental element for all living organisms
Involves processes like photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition, and combustion
Maintains balance of CO₂ in atmosphere
Key cycle linked to climate change

notes.heading: Processes in Carbon Cycle
points: Photosynthesis – plants absorb CO₂ and convert into organic matter
Respiration – organisms release CO₂ into atmosphere
Decomposition – breakdown of dead matter releases carbon
Combustion – burning of fossil fuels releases CO₂
Ocean absorption – oceans act as major carbon sink

notes.heading: Carbon Reservoirs
points: Atmosphere – CO₂ gas
Biosphere – plants and animals
Hydrosphere – dissolved carbon in oceans
Lithosphere – fossil fuels and carbonate rocks
Oceans store the largest amount of carbon

notes.heading: Human Impact on Carbon Cycle
points: Burning of fossil fuels increases atmospheric CO₂
Deforestation reduces carbon absorption
Industrial activities release greenhouse gases
Leads to global warming and climate change
Disturbs natural carbon balance

name: Nitrogen Cycle, Phosphorus Cycle & Sulphur Cycle

notes.heading: Overview
points: Biogeochemical cycles recycle essential nutrients through ecosystems
Nitrogen, phosphorus, and sulfur are key nutrient cycles for life processes
They maintain soil fertility, ecosystem productivity, and biological functions
Nitrogen and sulfur are gaseous cycles, while phosphorus is sedimentary

notes.heading: Nitrogen Cycle – Meaning
points: Nitrogen cycle describes movement of nitrogen between atmosphere, soil, and living organisms
Nitrogen is essential for proteins, DNA, and chlorophyll
Atmosphere contains about 78% nitrogen but it is unusable in free form
Conversion into usable forms is done by biological and physical processes
Maintains soil fertility and ecosystem productivity

notes.heading: Steps of Nitrogen Cycle
points: Nitrogen fixation – conversion of atmospheric N₂ into ammonia (by bacteria or lightning)
Nitrification – ammonia converted into nitrites and nitrates
Assimilation – plants absorb nitrates to form proteins
Ammonification – decomposition of organic matter releases ammonia
Denitrification – conversion of nitrates back to nitrogen gas

notes.heading: Importance of Nitrogen Cycle
points: Essential for protein synthesis in living organisms
Maintains soil fertility
Supports plant growth and agriculture
Maintains atmospheric balance of nitrogen
Prevents accumulation of toxic nitrogen compounds

notes.heading: Phosphorus Cycle – Meaning
points: Phosphorus cycle describes movement of phosphorus through rocks, soil, water, and organisms
Essential for DNA, ATP, and cell membranes
Unlike nitrogen, it does not have a gaseous phase
Main reservoir is sedimentary rocks and soil
Very slow cycling process

notes.heading: Steps of Phosphorus Cycle
points: Weathering of rocks releases phosphate into soil and water
Plants absorb phosphate from soil
Animals obtain phosphorus by consuming plants
Decomposition returns phosphorus to soil
Sedimentation stores phosphorus in rocks over time

notes.heading: Importance of Phosphorus Cycle
points: Essential for energy transfer (ATP)
Important for bone and teeth formation
Supports plant growth and root development
Critical for ecosystem productivity
Slow cycle makes it a limiting nutrient

notes.heading: Sulphur Cycle – Meaning
points: Sulphur cycle describes movement of sulfur through atmosphere, soil, water, and organisms
Important for protein structure (amino acids like cysteine and methionine)
Has both gaseous and sedimentary components
Sources include volcanic activity, fossil fuels, and decomposition
Plays role in ecosystem and atmospheric chemistry

notes.heading: Steps of Sulphur Cycle
points: Release from rocks through weathering and volcanic activity
Absorption by plants in form of sulfates
Transfer to animals through food chain
Decomposition returns sulfur to soil
Atmospheric sulfur dioxide converted into sulfuric acid (acid rain)

notes.heading: Importance of Sulphur Cycle
points: Essential for protein synthesis in organisms
Maintains soil fertility
Important in enzyme and vitamin structure
Influences atmospheric chemistry and acid rain formation
Supports ecosystem functioning

notes.heading: Nitrogen vs Phosphorus vs Sulphur Cycle
points: Nitrogen – gaseous cycle with atmospheric reservoir
Phosphorus – sedimentary cycle with no gaseous phase
Sulphur – both gaseous and sedimentary components
Nitrogen cycle is fastest, phosphorus is slowest
All are essential for biological processes
